paragraph: Specifying the scope of use of a dataset is an important step before sharing it [ 41]. Particularly, it is known that data-driven models are not reliable and may be unfair towards the groups that are not well represented in their (training) dataset [ 36,37]. Therefore, it is im- portant to identify the potential groups that are under-represented ∗This work was supported in part by the National Science Foundation, Grant No. 2348919 and 2107290. However, data in practice often misses to include demographic information of entities. Even in cases where some demographic information are available, many others may be missing that is necessary for identifying representa- tion bias [ 38]. To further motivate this problem, let us consider the following example: Example 1. A data-sharing platform (e.g., Chicago Open Data Portal [2]) would like to responsibly specify the under-represented andunder-performing groups in their shared data in order to limit their scope of use. However, their datasets either do not include grouping attributes (such as race) or only contain some of those. Moreover, targeting a comprehensive audit, they do not want to limit their scope to a small set of predefined groups. Instead, they want to be proactive in their detection process, even for the groups they might have missed to consider. For some cases such as image datasets, when a small and prede- termined set of grouping attributes (e.g., gender ) are missing, one may be able to use techniques such as crowdsourcing to identify under-represented groups based on those attributes [ 31]. Our prob- lem, however, is that the grouping attributes are not predetermined. In other words, we consider an unknown unknown situation where not only do we lack access to the grouping attributes but we also do not know the groups of interest. To address this problem, we introduce the problem of mining the potential groups that are under-represented and under-performing, when the grouping attributes are unknown. We refer to this prob- lem as Minoria mining . To the best of our knowledge, this paper isthe first to introduce and study the Minoria mining problem . In simple terms, the main question we want to answer in this paper is, “are there regions in data-space, representing potential groups that are (a) under-represented, for which (b) the model under-performs ?” For instance, aligned with Example 1, our experi- ments on a Crimes dataset (§ 7.1.1) identified North-side Chicago as under-represented and under-performing. This information helps the model developers and data owners such as Chicago Open Data Portal to proactively identify a potential issue, decide if it is socially concerning, and limit the dataset’s scope-of-use accordingly. Similar to any other data mining problem, multiple approaches may come to mind for addressing this problem. For example, one can adapt a clustering technique (such as k-means clustering [ 28] or subspace and projective clustering [ 24,29,32]) to cluster the data into potential groups. However, as we shall show in our experi- ments (§ 7.1.2) such an approach fails to identify under-represented groups, simply because there are not enough instances from those groups in the dataset. This is a well-known drawback of the clus- tering methods, that their performance degrades substantially for

Moreover, targeting a comprehensive audit, they do not want to limit their scope to a small set of predefined groups. Instead, they want to be proactive in their detection process, even for the groups they might have missed to consider. For some cases such as image datasets, when a small and prede- termined set of grouping attributes (e.g., gender ) are missing, one may be able to use techniques such as crowdsourcing to identify under-represented groups based on those attributes [ 31]. Our prob- lem, however, is that the grouping attributes are not predetermined. In other words, we consider an unknown unknown situation where not only do we lack access to the grouping attributes but we also do not know the groups of interest. To address this problem, we introduce the problem of mining the potential groups that are under-represented and under-performing, when the grouping attributes are unknown. We refer to this prob- lem as Minoria mining . To the best of our knowledge, this paper isthe first to introduce and study the Minoria mining problem . In simple terms, the main question we want to answer in this paper is, “are there regions in data-space, representing potential groups that are (a) under-represented, for which (b) the model under-performs ?” For instance, aligned with Example 1, our experi- ments on a Crimes dataset (§ 7.1.1) identified North-side Chicago as under-represented and under-performing. This information helps the model developers and data owners such as Chicago Open Data Portal to proactively identify a potential issue, decide if it is socially concerning, and limit the dataset’s scope-of-use accordingly. Similar to any other data mining problem, multiple approaches may come to mind for addressing this problem. For example, one can adapt a clustering technique (such as k-means clustering [ 28] or subspace and projective clustering [ 24,29,32]) to cluster the data into potential groups. However, as we shall show in our experi- ments (§ 7.1.2) such an approach fails to identify under-represented groups, simply because there are not enough instances from those groups in the dataset. Summary of contributions . In this paper, we introduce and for- malize the Minoria mining problem. We propose an approach for the problem based on the high-skew projections in the feature space that reflect performance-disparities at the projection tail. It turns combination”.out that finding such projections is challenging as it requires iden- tifying the median of each projection. To address this challenge, we utilize computational geometry notions such as duality, k-th level of arrangement, and the arrangement skeleton, and define the concept of median regions [ 21]. We prove the sufficient condi- tions for finding the maximum skew within each median region, which enables developing an efficient Ray-sweeping algorithm for a constant number of dimensions. Our Ray-sweeping algorithm hasthe same time complexity as of the k-th level of arrangement enumeration. This algorithm, however, suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Therefore, we propose practical solutions such as search-space discretization and smart exploration of the search space for large-scale high-dimensional settings. Besides theoretical guarantees, our experiments on multiple datasets confirm the va- lidity of our proposal and the performance of our algorithms. For example, our experiments on a Chicago crime dataset discovered an under-preforming high-skew projection that (mostly) reflects thewhite group.

In this section, we start by studying the problem in R2– referred to as the 2D case. Before providing the technical details, we would like to clarify that in the 2D case, Dcan have more than two observation attributes (used for prediction). However, the projection directions are considered with respect to a pair of observation attributes called attributes of interest. For example, in our experiments in § 7, we uselongitude and latitude as the attributes of interest for Minoria mining in a crime dataset. Recall that our goal is to find a set of high-skew directions. Let H={d(ti)|ti∈D} be the set of dual hyper-planes in the dual space and letEbe an oracle that returns An 2(the ordered list of vertices in then 2-th level of arrangement of H) inTenum time. GivenAn 2, we can iterate through the neighboring median re- gions by iterating through the elements (vertices) of this ordered list. Based on Theorem 2, within each median region, the high-skew direction is either at the boundary points (two vertices of the line 4Due to the space limitations, the proof is provided in the technical report [16]. segment) or at a specific direction, which can be calculated in O(d). Since this time is dominated by the time taken to calculate the skew value of the directions corresponding to the boundary points, we can ignore it while analyzing the complexity of our algorithm. In the second phase of our algorithm, we should iterate through the neighboring median regions and calculate the skew value of the directions of the boundaries of these regions. We want to return the top-lhigh-skew directions as the Minoria candidates. In order to do that, we use a Max-Heap data structure to push these directions based on their skew value. We define Tskew as the running time of this phase. In the end, we pop the top- ldirections from the heap, evaluate the model on the tail of these directions, and check the error on the tail to see if it represents an under-represented group candidate. A visualization of this approach is provided in Figure 3. LetTpopbe the time complexity of the final step. Then, the overall time complexity of the algorithm is T=Tenum+Tskew+Tpop. The generalized Ray-sweeping algorithm suffers from the curse of dimensionality [21]. Therefore, in this section, we propose practical solutions based on search-space discretization (§ 6.1) and smart exploration of the projection space (§ 6.2 and 6.3).

Search-space discretization is common for addressing the curse of dimensionality. Following this idea, we propose two approaches to discretize the space of all possible directions finRdand find the high-skew projections in the discretized space. Our first strategy is uniform discretization, where the continuous space of all directions fis partitioned into equal-size grids, and uniformly distributed samples are taken from the grid. The second strategy works by incrementally building a set of ldirections using Quadratic Pro- gramming (QP), where the constraints of the QP are adjusted to enforce exploring the directions farthest from each other. we only focus on the positive partition of Rd. In this section, we evaluate the higher-dimensional methods pro- posed in § 6. As reflected in our negative result on the error-bound of the discretization approaches [ 16], their effectiveness depends on the dataset topology. Besides, their running time significantly in- creases by the number of dimensions. Our experiments verify these findings: we found discretization slow and less effective. There- fore, in the following we focus on the more practical approaches based on the search space exploration. Comparing the E&E method (§ 6.2) and the focused exploration approach (§ 6.3), our experiments found the latter (focused exploration) significantly more effective for Minoria mining. Therefore, in the following, we first present our results for this approach and then present our extended experiment results for the E&E approach and highlight some of its drawbacks. 7.2.1 Focused Exploration. We ran experiments on three real-world datasets. The Adult Income Dataset [ 20] consists of demographic information for individuals, from the 1994 Census database. The dataset is primarily used to predict whether a person earns more than $50,000 per year based on various attributes (14 columns and 48,842 rows). Gender is the sensitive attribute in this dataset. The COMPAS dataset [ 7] contains data used to evaluate the effective- ness and fairness of the COMPAS recidivism prediction algorithm. This dataset includes criminal history, jail and prison time, demo- graphics, and COMPAS risk scores for defendants from Broward County, Florida (52 columns and 18,316 rows). Race is the sensitive attribute in this dataset. The last dataset is the Diabetes dataset [ 40]. This is a well-known dataset used for binary classification tasks in the medical domain. Addressing representation biases in datasets is a well-studied issue in the literature. Existing methods study the detection and resolu- tion of representation bias for discrete and continuous data with various modalities [ 38]. The literature also includes statistical and classical methods for identifying patterns and gaps corresponding to empty spaces within the dataset [22, 26, 27].

Several studies have been conducted to identify the underper- forming regions of machine learning models [ 14,33,35,43]. Thesestudies aim to detect regions and sub-spaces that present challenges for the model in making accurate predictions. SliceFinder [ 14] de- tects specific “slices” of data where a machine learning model un- derperforms, indicated by a significantly higher average loss on these slices compared to other parts of the dataset. Other methods build on this concept by concentrating on specific regions of the data [ 35]. Chen et al. [ 12] employ clustering approaches to identify partitions of data that are discriminated against by a classification model. They aim to discover clusters where the model’s perfor- mance varies between demographic groups. The issue of identifying underrepresented groups within a sampled population is explored by Lancia et al. [ 25], who focus on detecting poorly represented groups and resampling these hard-to-sample sub-groups. Pastor et al. [ 33] also introduce a concept of pattern divergence to exam- ine a model’s behavior across different sub-populations. Existing work also includes [ 31] that combines crowdsourcing and machine learning to detect uncovered groups over predetermined grouping attributes on image datasets without explicit group information. The primary distinction between our work and the existing literature is that we assume no prior information about the group- ing attributes within the dataset. In other words, we aim to mine Minoria from a collection of data points without explicit access to demographic group information over predetermined grouping attributes. Our goal is to identify the groups that are unknown, underrepresented, and underperforming for a given prediction task.
